summary: Defines new IKEv2 notification status types so a responder can tell the initiator which address families, IPv4 or IPv6, are allowed. This helps manage IPv4 and IPv6 coexistence on VPN connections, and updates RFC 7296.

plainLanguage.summary: When setting up a secure tunnel, one side can say you may use the old kind of address, the new kind, or both.

questions: how does ikev2 signal allowed address families
subtitle: New IKEv2 notifications let a VPN responder tell the initiator which of IPv4 and IPv6 it will hand out.

tldr.problem: When an IKEv2 initiator asks for IPv4 and/or IPv6 addresses, the only generic failure signal is INTERNAL_ADDRESS_FAILURE, which does not say why an address family was not assigned or what to try next.
tldr.mechanism: The responder adds IP4_ALLOWED and/or IP6_ALLOWED notification status types to its response, following a table that maps what was requested and supported to what is returned. The initiator uses them to decide whether to ask again.
tldr.outcome: Initiators get deterministic behavior for address-family mismatches. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 7296 and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 8983 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2021. It updates RFC 7296 and has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 8983 adds two small notification status types to IKEv2, the key exchange protocol defined in RFC 7296. They let the responder tell the initiator which IP address families (IPv4 or IPv6) it allows.

The motivating case comes from cellular networks. A phone attached through a non-3GPP access network such as a WLAN has no IKEv2 notification that explains why an address family was not assigned, or whether it should retry with the other one. The RFC fills that gap, and notes that the new types are not specific to 3GPP and can be used in other deployments.
sections.plainLanguage: Two computers set up a private tunnel. This RFC gives one of them a way to say which kinds of addresses it is willing to give out.

sections.title: The Cellular Precedent
sections.content:
Per RFC 7849, if subscription data or network configuration allows only one address family, a cellular host must not request a second PDP-Context to the same Access Point Name for the other family. The 3GPP network says what is allowed using Session Management cause codes:

  • #50 "PDP type IPv4 only allowed"
  • #51 "PDP type IPv6 only allowed"
  • #52 "single address bearers only allowed"

If a requested IPv4v6 PDP-Context is not supported but both IPv4 and IPv6 PDP types are allowed, the host gets one family and must start a second PDP-Context for the other, to reach dual-stack connectivity with two PDP-Contexts. IKEv2 had nothing equivalent.
sections.plainLanguage: Phone networks already tell your phone which kinds of connections it may use. The tunnel protocol had no way to say the same thing.

sections.title: Why Not INTERNAL_ADDRESS_FAILURE?
sections.content:
An initiator can hit several address assignment failures: it asks for one family the responder does not support, asks for both but only IPv4 or only IPv6 can be assigned, or asks for both but policy lets the responder assign only one.

Section 3.15.4 of RFC 7296 defines the generic error INTERNAL_ADDRESS_FAILURE, and the responder sends it only if no addresses can be assigned. It is a catch-all, so it does not tell the initiator why a family was not assigned or whether to try another. The RFC concludes it does not give enough hints for the initiator to adjust its behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: Saying only "something went wrong with addresses" is like a shop that just says "no". You still do not know what to ask for instead.

sections.title: IP4_ALLOWED and IP6_ALLOWED
sections.content:
IP4_ALLOWED and IP6_ALLOWED are notification status types that inform the initiator about the responder's address family assignment support and report why an assignment failed. The initiator uses them to adjust its behavior.

No data is associated with either notification. Their presence is the whole message.
sections.plainLanguage: They are like two little flags the responder can raise: one for the older kind of address, one for the newer kind.

sections.title: Responder and Initiator Behavior
sections.content:
A dual-stack initiator MUST include configuration attributes for both address families in its configuration request, unless explicit policy or configuration says otherwise. The responder MUST include IP6_ALLOWED and/or IP4_ALLOWED in its response, as the table below shows.

The initiator then follows these rules:

  • If it receives just one IP4_ALLOWED or IP6_ALLOWED, it MUST NOT send a later request for the other family.
  • If a dual-stack initiator asked for only one family and receives only the notification for the other, it MUST send a request for the other family.
  • If it asked for both, got one family, and received both notifications, it MAY ask for the other family, but then MUST create a new IKE Security Association and ask on that.

For other address-related errors, both sides follow Section 3.15.4 of RFC 7296.
sections.plainLanguage: If the doorman says only one kind of pass exists, do not ask for the other. If you asked for the wrong one, ask for the right one. If both exist but you only got one, you may start a fresh visit to get the other.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says that a node's IPv4/IPv6 capabilities are readily determined from the traffic it generates. It therefore introduces no new security considerations compared with RFC 7296, whose considerations continue to apply.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone watching can already tell which kinds of addresses a computer uses, so these flags reveal nothing new.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA has added two entries to the "IKEv2 Notify Message Types - Status Types" registry: IP4_ALLOWED with value 16439 and IP6_ALLOWED with value 16440, both referencing RFC 8983.
sections.plainLanguage: Each flag got an official number in the public list of IKEv2 messages, so everyone uses the same ones.
